findings.headline: Remaining divestment and asset disposal resources forecast insufficient to reduce borrowing without additional government support
findings.detail: Over £700m has been raised from divestment and disposal programmes to date. However, the report projects that remaining resources will be inadequate to reduce the Capital Financing Requirement (£1.071bn) without additional government support beyond the £200m relief package.
findings.matters: There is no self-help path to sustainability. The council is entirely dependent on whether government support continues beyond current commitments.
findings.figures: Over £700m raised to date; total CFR £1,071m
findings.quote: The forecast level of Council resources from the divestment and asset disposals programme is expected to be insufficient to provide a future fall in the CFR without additional Government support

findings.headline: Financing costs consume one-third of non-HRA revenue, leaving minimal capacity for service spending or reserve building
findings.detail: Treasury financing costs (debt interest and minimum revenue provision) represent 35.2% of non-HRA net revenue (£59.2m of £168.5m) and 31.5% of HRA revenue. The report explicitly identifies this as reinforcing the 'unsustainable budget predicament.'
findings.matters: One-third of revenue consumed by debt servicing is a stark indicator of unaffordability. No service improvements or reserves accumulation is possible when legacy debt dominates the budget.
findings.figures: Non-HRA financing costs 35.2% (£59.2m of £168.5m); HRA 31.5% (£20.2m of £64.1m)
findings.quote: the annual financing costs for the non-HRA are approximately a third of net revenue. This percentage reinforces the unsustainable budget predicament

findings.headline: Major asset sales (wind farm disposals c£40m) slipped from 2024/25 to 2026/27, delaying reduction in the borrowing requirement
findings.detail: The Council budgeted £6.175m in divestment receipts for 2025/26 but achieved only £1.752m. Most significantly, two wind farm disposals expected in late 2024/25 have slipped by a full year to 2026/27. These c£40m proceeds are central to reducing the Capital Financing Requirement.
findings.matters: Disposal slippage directly extends the period of government dependence and increases the risk that conditions for the £200m relief package cannot be met. Further slippage would materially worsen the financial outlook.
findings.figures: Wind farm disposals c£40m delayed one year; actual receipts £1.752m vs budget £6.175m
findings.quote: The two delayed wind farm disposals (c£40m) initially expected in late 2024/25 are now expected during 2026/27.

findings.headline: Interest rates rose above 6% versus forecast 4.80%, and 75% of debt is short-term, creating significant refinancing risk
findings.detail: Treasury advisors forecast longer-term PWLB rates would fall to 4.80%. Instead, geopolitical factors caused rates to rise above 6% in late 2025/26. With 75% of the debt portfolio in short-term funds, refinancing risk is high—a rate spike would immediately increase servicing costs and compress the already tight budget.
findings.matters: The council's debt costs are highly vulnerable to further rate increases. Actual rates diverging significantly from forecasts undermines the credibility of financial projections and shows real-time exposure to market conditions.
findings.figures: 75% of debt portfolio short-term; actual PWLB rates above 6% vs forecast 4.80%
findings.quote: Due to geo-political reasons late in 2025/26, primarily in the Middle east, whilst short term interest rates have fallen, this has not been as fast as originally expected and longer term fixed PWLB interest rates have risen above 6%, rather than the forecasted fall to 4.80%.

findings.headline: Council cannot balance its budget without ongoing exceptional government support; structural deficit driven by legacy debt costs
findings.detail: The annual deficit of £59.1m in 2025/26 is primarily composed of £52.2m in treasury management costs (debt interest and minimum revenue provision). Without the capitalisation direction from MHCLG, the council cannot operate a balanced budget. This is not a forecasting variance but a structural reality.
findings.matters: The deficit cannot be closed by service reductions or efficiency gains alone; it is entirely driven by legacy commercial investment debt. Financial sustainability requires either continued government support or massive asset sales.
findings.figures: Annual deficit £59.1m; treasury costs £52.2m; capitalisation direction £59.1m
findings.quote: This Council cannot currently operate a balanced budget without exceptional external support from the MHCLG through the annual capitalisation direction (CD). The budget deficit is primarily due to the treasury management costs (MRP and debt interest costs) associated with the historic commercial investment programme. In 2025/26 these £52.2m treasury management costs form the main part of the Council's estimated annual deficit (£59.1m)

findings.headline: £200m government debt relief is conditional and formal approval has not yet been issued
findings.detail: Central Government committed in-principle to repay £200m of non-HRA debt in 2026/27, subject to further assurance of the Council's financial position, continued asset disposals, and other local actions. The report explicitly notes that formal approval and implementation details have yet to be issued, creating uncertainty over both timing and whether conditions can be met.
findings.matters: This relief is the linchpin of the council's recovery plan. Any failure to meet conditions or delay in formal approval directly impacts both the sustainability timeline and the credibility of the finance strategy.
findings.figures: £200m in-principle commitment for 2026/27
findings.quote: In recognising the progress that has been made to reduce debt, the government has announced an in-principle commitment to repay £200m of the Council's debt in 2026/27. This support is subject to further assurance of the Council's financial position, continued progress on remaining asset disposals and divestments as well as other local actions to strengthen financial sustainability.

findings.headline: Income-dependent savings showing weak underlying delivery, masked by mitigation from parking income and property-related decisions
findings.detail: Moving Traffic Offences (£333k) is marked delivered but commentary states 'Saving not achieved' and was mitigated by 'surplus Parking income' in 25-26; this same saving 'is to be reversed out in 26-27'. Weekend Enforcement (£17k) earned 'no income in 25-26 due to timescales to recruit'. Household Waste Recycling (£127k) is 'almost entirely mitigated' and depends on a newly operational weigh bridge.
findings.matters: New enforcement and waste income streams are delivering below plan or inconsistently, and the council is plugging gaps with parking income that may not be stable or sustained
findings.figures: Moving Traffic Offences: £333k (not achieved, to reverse in 26-27), Weekend Enforcement: £17k (no income earned), Household Waste: £127k (mitigated)
findings.quote: P12 - Saving not achieved but mitigated by underspends on Selective Licencing staff + surplus Parking income in 25-26. This unchievable saving is to be reversed out in 26-27

findings.headline: Grangewaters leisure income target dramatically underperformed at only 24% of £150k saving despite system going live mid-year
findings.detail: The council targeted £150k in commercialisation savings from Grangewaters but delivered only £35,612 (a 76% shortfall). The new website and online booking system were implemented in September 2025, but have not yet driven expected income growth. The council is managing the 2025-26 shortfall 'as a one off' and betting on recovery in summer 2026.
findings.matters: A major income-generation initiative delivered a quarter of target despite being live for half the year, suggesting demand or pricing issues, and relies on unproven recovery in 2026-27
findings.figures: £150,000 target, £35,612 delivered (24% of target), £114,388 shortfall
findings.quote: The website and online booking system was implemented September 2025, which has impacted on income earned. All opportunities continue to be explored to increase footfall and income.

findings.headline: Finance department agency staff overspends are consuming restructure savings despite recent permanent staff reduction
findings.detail: The Finance Team restructure completed end of 2024-25 achieved £200k in permanent savings by deleting vacant posts. However, the same section is 'incurring significant overspends on agency staff'. The commentary explicitly notes the permanent savings were delivered 'although there are significant overspends on agency staff within the Finance department'.
findings.matters: Finance team instability (needing agency cover despite a restructure) creates operational risk for the council's own financial controls and budget management, and the agency spend is reversing the restructure benefit
findings.figures: £200,000 permanent savings offset by unquantified agency staff overspends
findings.quote: The savings to the permanent team structure have been delivered, although there are significant overspends on agency staff within the Finance department.

findings.headline: Multiple Adult Social Care savings only delivered through overachievement in other ASC areas, creating fragile interdependencies
findings.detail: Several ASC savings marked 'Mitigated' depend on overachievement of Assistive Technology charging and CHC income. Moving with Dignity (£109k) and Occupational Therapy (£100k) note staff onboarded late. Daycare service fees (£512k) are marked 'partly at risk' with the caveat that 'full achievement of the saving may not be realised'.
findings.matters: When savings depend on mitigation from other areas, underperformance cascades: if CHC income or assistive technology overachievement falls short, multiple other supposedly 'delivered' or 'mitigated' savings collapse
findings.figures: £512k (Daycare fees partly at risk), £109k (Moving with Dignity mitigated), £100k (OT mitigated), mitigated by £140k overachievement on assistive technology
findings.quote: Partly at risk; charges have been invoiced but full achievement of the saving may not be realised. Mitigated by overachievement in CHC income.

findings.headline: Three major transformation savings totalling £730k are unachievable and must be reversed from the MTFS
findings.detail: Strategic Commissioning (£200k), Digital Redesign (£300k), and Contact Management (£230k) savings have not been delivered in 2025-26. The council explicitly states all three 'will need to be reversed as part of the MTFS', creating a structural £730k budget shortfall that must be replaced elsewhere in the plan.
findings.matters: Unachievable transformation savings suggest the council's change programme is not delivering at planned pace, forcing the council to find alternative cuts or income in-year or defer the gap to future years
findings.figures: £200,000 (Strategic Commissioning), £300,000 (Digital Redesign), £230,000 (Contact Management), plus £100k (Print Outsourcing) = £830k total unachievable
findings.quote: This saving is currently deemed unachievable in this financial year, so will need to be reversed as part of the MTFS.

findings.headline: Favourable treasury outturn (£10.104m underspend) driven by one-off factors including capital slippage and favourable conditions, not structural improvement
findings.detail: The largest driver of the improved outturn is a £10.104m underspend on Treasury Management, comprising £7.303m from commercial income, £6.194m interest payable underspend, offset by £3.394m MRP pressure. The paper notes these are 'non-recurring' and that 'a proportion of these variances are non-recurring, and the MTFS will need to reflect underlying financing costs on a sustainable basis'.
findings.matters: The outturn looks better than the underlying structural position because of timing and one-off gains. Next year will see these reverse, making the underlying structural deficit apparent unless demand-led pressures are addressed.
findings.figures: £10.104m treasury underspend; £7.303m commercial income variance; £6.194m interest payable underspend
findings.quote: A proportion of these variances are non-recurring, and the MTFS will need to reflect underlying financing costs on a sustainable basis.

findings.headline: No Recourse to Public Funds (NRPF) overspend of £0.707m where council has statutory duty to house families, creating non-discretionary demand pressure
findings.detail: Children's Services overspent by £0.707m on NRPF, where 'the Council has a statutory duty to house homeless families with dependent children and provide financial subsistence'. This is a non-discretionary service where the council cannot refuse demand. The paper notes this is being mitigated through grant maximisation and savings, but the underlying demand exists.
findings.matters: NRPF is a statutory duty with no funding source. Any growth in numbers or costs cannot be reduced without legal breach. This represents a hard-to-control expenditure growth area.
findings.figures: £0.707m NRPF overspend
findings.quote: No Recourse to Public Funds (NRPF) is £0.707m overspent where the Council has a statutory duty to house homeless families with dependent children and provide financial subsistence.

findings.headline: Capital programme delivering only 27% of revised budget in General Fund (£87.462m underspend on £120.250m), raising delivery questions
findings.detail: The General Fund capital programme underspent by £87.462m (73% of revised budget), of which £82.051m relates to slippage. Major programmes in regeneration, infrastructure and schools are delayed due to 'procurement delays, planning requirements and programme dependencies'. A deep-dive review of slippage is being undertaken and will report to Cabinet.
findings.matters: Persistent capital slippage suggests the council's delivery capability is constrained. While lower spend reduces short-term borrowing, it also delays schemes that may address long-term service capacity or regeneration objectives.
findings.figures: £87.462m underspend (73%); £82.051m slippage; £5.411m reduced programme spend
findings.quote: The General Fund Capital programme reports an £87.462m underspend (73%) against a revised budget of £120.250m... Slippage on major regeneration, infrastructure and school expansion schemes due to procurement delays, planning requirements and programme dependencies.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account repairs overspend of £1.178m from backlog works and compliance, signalling asset condition issues
findings.detail: The HRA reported repairs overspend of £1.178m arising from 'backlog works, higher void costs, and increased compliance activity'. This is described as an 'operational pressure' that 'will need to be managed alongside financing assumptions within the HRA business plan'. The HRA holds £13.511m in balances, but ongoing structural repairs pressure threatens this.
findings.matters: HRA repairs backlog is a symptom of deferred investment and rising compliance costs. It signals deteriorating housing stock condition and future capital needs that may not be fundable.
findings.figures: £1.178m repairs overspend; HRA balances £13.511m
findings.quote: Repairs & Maintenance: £1.178m overspend arising from backlog works, higher void costs, and increased compliance activity.

findings.headline: Council's reliance on reserves to manage short-term pressures acknowledged as unsustainable medium-term
findings.detail: The council is making a net contribution to reserves of £11.063m in 2025/26 (£25.969m contributions, £13.329m drawdowns), bringing total reserves to £82.137m. However, the paper explicitly states: 'The use of reserves reflects the Council's planned approach to managing financial pressures in the short term. However, this reliance on reserves is not sustainable over the medium term.' Reserves are being used to bridge structural demand overspends.
findings.matters: Reserves are finite and being consumed to mask structural overspends rather than to cover genuine contingencies. Once exhausted, the council has no buffer for adverse movements in demand-led services.
findings.figures: £11.063m net contribution to reserves; total reserves £82.137m; drawing down £13.329m to fund services
findings.quote: The use of reserves reflects the Council's planned approach to managing financial pressures in the short term. However, this reliance on reserves is not sustainable over the medium term.

findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support requirement of £59.070m remains despite improved outturn, reflecting structural deficit not operational performance
findings.detail: The council required £59.070m in capitalisation direction to balance 2025/26, down from £72.128m budgeted but still £3.040m higher than Q3 revised forecast. The improvement comes from treasury underspend (£10.104m) and unused contingency (£5.103m), not from operational improvements. The commissioners note this is 'indicative at this stage' and subject to audit conclusion.
findings.matters: This level of EFS signals the council cannot balance its budget from revenues and is dependent on government capitalisation to cover structural deficits. It is the clearest indicator of financial distress.
findings.figures: £59.070m EFS requirement; down from £72.128m budgeted; £10.104m from treasury underspend
findings.quote: The provisional outturn for the Total Operating budget is £231.439m... This would require Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) of £59.070m, a reduction of £13.058m from when the budget was set in February 2025

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant accumulated deficit forecast at £42.530m by 2028/29, driven by sustained EHCP volume and complexity growth
findings.detail: The DSG overspent by £5.302m in 2025/26 (7.37% of budget) on a revised budget of £71.977m, with the High Needs Block accounting for most of the pressure. The council's own management plan forecasts this will balloon to a cumulative £42.530m deficit by 2028/29. While government reform proposals may cover 90% of deficit, this is not yet confirmed.
findings.matters: A £42.5m cumulative funding gap across a three-year horizon, even if partly covered by government, represents a material structural liability that will either consume reserves or drive additional EFS requests
findings.figures: £5.302m 2025/26 overspend; cumulative forecast deficit of £42.530m by 2028/29; High Needs Block £6.251m overspend
findings.quote: The DSG Management Plan forecasts a cumulative deficit of £42.530m by 2028/29, highlighting a significant structural funding gap driven by sustained demand growth.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspend of £3.178m deteriorated by £3.783m since quarter 3, with no permanent funding solution secured beyond 2026/27
findings.detail: The directorate overspent by £3.178m, primarily due to £1.659m pressure on external placements from increased demand and complexity. The paper explicitly states this represents an 'ongoing cost pressure with implications for future financial sustainability' and notes that 'a permanent solution will be required from 2027/28'. If in-year control fails, reserves will be used.
findings.matters: Structural demand-led overspends that cannot be solved through contingency or treasury gains create persistent borrowing needs and draw down reserves unsustainably
findings.figures: £3.178m overspend; deterioration of £3.783m since Q3; £1.659m external placements pressure
findings.quote: The £3.178m overspend represents an ongoing cost pressure with implications for future financial sustainability... A permanent solution will be required from 2027/28 to ensure the budget is sustainable through the MTFS process.

findings.paper_title: Thurrock Council's DRAFT 2025-26 Annual Governance Statement , item 106.
findings.headline: PWE Holdings investment now represents 94% equity stake following refinancing
findings.detail: The council originally invested £30m in PWE Holdings bonds in 2018. Following refinancing and maturity, most debt was converted to equity, leaving the council as 94% owner of PWE with £2m debt still being repaid as a loan. This is a large, concentrated equity position in a private company.
findings.matters: The council has a large illiquid equity stake in a private company. This represents potential write-down risk and ties up capital that could otherwise be deployed to reduce borrowing.
findings.figures: Council owns 94% of PWE; £2m outstanding loan; originally invested £30m in bonds
findings.quote: The Council originally invested £30 m in bonds in PWE Holdings in three tranches in 2018. £20 m was outstanding when the bonds matured in December 2020. Following a refinancing the Council received a payment of £1m debt in 2022. The Council retained a debt of £2m which is being repaid as a loan, but the remainder of the debt was converted to equity making the Council the majority (94%) owner of PWE.

findings.paper_title: Thurrock Council's DRAFT 2025-26 Annual Governance Statement , item 106.
findings.headline: Records management migration to SharePoint is behind schedule
findings.detail: Internal Audit review in September 2025 found concerns about storage, retention, and volume of documents. The council is migrating data to SharePoint but the project 'is behind schedule and may need additional resources particularly due to the volumes and lack of clarity with some of the boxes and documents retained.'
findings.matters: Poor records management creates regulatory risk (GDPR, FOI, SAR), audit risk, and discovery risk in litigation. Lack of clarity about what is retained suggests poor information governance.
findings.figures: Records migration project behind schedule
findings.quote: There is a migration project for transferring data to Sharepoint but this is behind schedule and may need additional resources particularly due to the volumes and lack of clarity with some of the boxes and documents retained.

findings.paper_title: Thurrock Council's DRAFT 2025-26 Annual Governance Statement , item 106.
findings.headline: Sickness days per full-time equivalent increased during the year
findings.detail: The statement reports that 'the number of sickness days per FTE has increased throughout the year and in comparison, to last year.' While still at benchmark levels, the trend is upward and the council is working to manage high-impact long-term cases.
findings.matters: Rising sickness suggests either increasing stress on workforce during transformation, or deteriorating workplace conditions. High sickness reduces productivity and increases pressure on tight staffing levels.
findings.figures: Sickness days per FTE increased year-on-year; level in line with benchmarks
findings.quote: Whilst sickness is in line with benchmark comparators, the number of sickness days per FTE has increased throughout the year and in comparison, to last year.

findings.paper_title: Thurrock Council's DRAFT 2025-26 Annual Governance Statement , item 106.
findings.headline: Average weekly cost of children's external placements rose from £2,500 to £2,912
findings.detail: The cost per placement for children in external care has increased by over 16%, indicating rising complexity of need and cost pressure. The council is seeking to develop more local provision but progress is constrained by shortage of regulated placements and proximity to London's higher costs.
findings.matters: Rising placement costs are a direct revenue pressure. If unable to develop local provision or shift demand to lower-cost options, this will continue to pressure budget.
findings.figures: Q4 average placement cost £2,912, compared with £2,500 in previous year
findings.quote: The overall needs of children in Thurrock Council's care continue to increase, resulting in a sustained requirement for higher‑cost care packages. This pressure is reflected in the Q4 average placement cost, which has remained high at £2,912, compared with £2,500 in the previous year, demonstrating the ongoing financial impact of increasing complexity.

findings.paper_title: Thurrock Council's DRAFT 2025-26 Annual Governance Statement , item 106.
findings.headline: Subsidiary company TRL lacks council oversight and winding-up is being considered
findings.detail: The council recognises 'an absence of oversight and grip by the Council on TRL' (Thurrock Regeneration Limited). External advisors have been appointed to assess options including whether the company can be wound up. TRL was set up in 2013 and funded by loans and land sold from the council.
findings.matters: A subsidiary company funded by council loans and land sales but lacking oversight represents both a governance failure and potential financial exposure. Winding-up may crystallise losses.
findings.figures: TRL is a wholly owned regeneration company; subsidiary Thurrock Regeneration Homes Ltd incorporated in 2017
findings.quote: It is recognised that there is an absence of oversight and grip by the Council on TRL and there is a piece of work being taken forward about future planning and what happens to the subsidiary company, including whether it can be wound up.

findings.paper_title: Thurrock Council's DRAFT 2025-26 Annual Governance Statement , item 106.
findings.headline: External auditors report council not responsive to audit information requests
findings.detail: Ernst and Young reported that the council had issues with 'the responsiveness of officers to requests for information and the meeting of informal deadlines.' The Chief Finance Officer had to implement changes to improve working arrangements.
findings.matters: Slow response to auditors suggests either weak management discipline or understaffing. Either way, it slows audit and increases audit risk.
findings.figures: 11 urgency notices used during the year
findings.quote: Ernst and Young (EY), highlighted issues they had experienced in working with the council on the 2024/25 audit during the course of this year, including the responsiveness of officers to requests for information and the meeting of informal deadlines.

findings.paper_title: Thurrock Council's DRAFT 2025-26 Annual Governance Statement , item 106.
findings.headline: Internal Audit gave LIMITED ASSURANCE on governance and controls
findings.detail: The Head of Internal Audit gave a 'LIMITED ASSURANCE' opinion on the adequacy and effectiveness of the organisation's framework of governance, risk management and control. This is the lowest assurance level and indicates significant control weaknesses.
findings.matters: Limited assurance means the council's control environment is materially weak. A lender cannot be confident that management controls are sufficient.
findings.figures: Limited Assurance opinion
findings.quote: The CAE's overall opinion on the adequacy and effectiveness of the organisation's framework of governance, risk management and control based on the annual review of governance and the assurance work of Internal Audit throughout 2025/26 is LIMITED ASSURANCE

findings.paper_title: Thurrock Council's DRAFT 2025-26 Annual Governance Statement , item 106.
findings.headline: Finance team cannot fill specialist posts on a permanent basis
findings.detail: The council identifies recruitment to 'specific hard to fill finance posts on a permanent basis' as a weakness. Officers acknowledge that 'there are still a number of open posts across finance in specific areas that have proven difficult to fill, and inevitably this could hamper further progress.'
findings.matters: A weak finance function cannot execute a £41m savings programme or manage debt reduction. Staffing gaps in finance are a direct threat to the council's recovery.
findings.figures: Multiple open posts in finance; permanent recruitment difficult
findings.quote: there are still a number of open posts across finance in specific areas that have proven difficult to fill, and inevitably this could hamper further progress.

findings.paper_title: Thurrock Council's DRAFT 2025-26 Annual Governance Statement , item 106.
findings.headline: Capital programme delivered only 27% of budget, with £87m slippage
findings.detail: The General Fund capital programme finished with a £87.5m underspend (73%) against revised budget of £120.25m. Of this, £82.2m slipped into future years. This suggests either overly optimistic planning or serious project management issues.
findings.matters: Large slippage indicates the council may struggle to execute its transformation and capital investment plans, which are part of its recovery strategy.
findings.figures: £87.462m underspend (73%) of £120.250m budget; £82.209m slippage to future years
findings.quote: The General Fund Capital Programme outturn reflects an underspend of £87.462m (73%) against the revised budget of £120.250m. Of this variance, £82.209m relates to slippage into future years

findings.paper_title: Thurrock Council's DRAFT 2025-26 Annual Governance Statement , item 106.
findings.headline: Reorganisation will combine debt of two councils with unknown disaggregation from county
findings.detail: Thurrock is being dissolved through local government reorganisation and merged with Basildon Council. The combined debt position is uncertain, and budget disaggregation from Essex County Council is unknown. This creates material financial risk during a period when debt reduction is a priority.
findings.matters: A lender to either council needs to understand the total debt exposure post-merger and whether there is a credible plan to manage it. The uncertainty itself is a risk.
findings.figures: Combined debt of Thurrock and Basildon; unknown value of budget disaggregation from Essex County Council
findings.quote: Additional work will be required to further understand and analyse the combined debt of both Thurrock and Basildon Councils alongside the unknown value of budget disaggregation from Essex County Council.

findings.paper_title: Thurrock Council's DRAFT 2025-26 Annual Governance Statement , item 106.
findings.headline: Medium-term financial strategy requires £41m of savings over three years
findings.detail: The council must find £41m in savings across three years to meet its legal duty to set balanced budgets, including £13.65m in 2026/27 alone. This is a large structural adjustment required from a unitary authority.
findings.matters: A finance director or lender evaluating affordability needs to know the scale and pace of the savings requirement and whether it is deliverable.
findings.figures: ~£41m over three years; £13.65m in savings in 2026/27
findings.quote: The Medium-Term Financial Strategy requires ~£41m over three years, including £13.65m in savings in 2026/27, to meet the legal duty to set a balanced budget.

findings.paper_title: Thurrock Council's DRAFT 2025-26 Annual Governance Statement , item 106.
findings.headline: Council still requires government bailout funding to set a balanced budget
findings.detail: Despite improvements under intervention since 2022, Thurrock continues to need Exceptional Financial Support to balance its budget. This is not a one-time issue but ongoing, indicating structural imbalance in the council's finances.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that this council cannot achieve a balanced budget without government subsidy, suggesting deep structural issues in revenue base or cost base.
findings.figures: Exceptional Financial Support still required; intervention extended to 30 April 2028
findings.quote: the continued requirement of Exceptional Financial Support in order to set a balanced budget

findings.paper_title: Updated Head of Internal Audit Opinion
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.thurrock.gov.uk/documents/b21814/Updated Head of Internal Audit Opinion 30th-Jun-2026 19.00 Audit Committee.pdf?T=9
findings.headline: Records Management received Limited Assurance and remains a significant improvement area
findings.detail: Records Management audit resulted in Limited Assurance opinion with 6 high-risk and 3 medium-risk recommendations. Issues included need to strengthen arrangements for physical archives, indexing, scanning, retention and wider records management compliance. The Council's Annual Governance Statement identifies Records Management as a continuing improvement area for 2026/27.
findings.matters: Weak records management means the council may lack audit trails, evidence of decisions, and documented compliance with procedures — undermining governance oversight and creating compliance risk.
findings.figures: Records Management audit: 6 high-risk recommendations, 3 medium-risk recommendations
findings.quote: Records Management received a Limited Assurance opinion and remains a significant area for improvement. Issues identified included the need to strengthen arrangements for physical archives, indexing, scanning, retention and wider records management compliance.

findings.paper_title: Updated Head of Internal Audit Opinion
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.thurrock.gov.uk/documents/b21814/Updated Head of Internal Audit Opinion 30th-Jun-2026 19.00 Audit Committee.pdf?T=9
findings.headline: High-risk and medium-risk audit recommendations are overdue: 12 out of 96 (5 high-risk, 7 medium-risk)
findings.detail: As of 31 March 2026, 12 audit recommendations that were due for implementation remain overdue: 5 high-risk and 7 medium-risk recommendations. Overall, only 78% of recommendations were implemented by their due date, missing the 90% target. The council is responsible for implementing recommendations.
findings.matters: Overdue implementation of high and medium-risk recommendations indicates management is not acting urgently on identified control weaknesses. This extends the period during which risks are materialising.
findings.figures: 55 high-risk recommendations: 35 implemented, 4 partially, 11 not due yet, 5 overdue. 41 medium-risk recommendations: 23 implemented, 1 partially, 10 not due yet, 7 overdue. Corporate PI target 90%, actual 78%
findings.quote: Risk Rating Total No of Recs Implemented Partially Implemented Not Due yet Overdue; High 55 35 4 11 5; Medium 41 23 1 10 7

findings.paper_title: Updated Head of Internal Audit Opinion
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.thurrock.gov.uk/documents/b21814/Updated Head of Internal Audit Opinion 30th-Jun-2026 19.00 Audit Committee.pdf?T=9
findings.headline: Four critical audits deferred to 2026/27: Financial Sustainability, Budget Management, Savings Assumptions, and Performance Management
findings.detail: Four audits originally in the 2025/26 plan were deferred: Financial Sustainability, Budget Management, Savings Assumptions and Plans, and Performance Management. The report explicitly states these areas remain significant to the Council's overall risk profile and acknowledges the deferral has been considered in reaching the Limited Assurance opinion.
findings.matters: Deferral of audits on financial sustainability, budget management and savings plans means the council has not been independently audited on these critical areas. For a lender, this is a major gap in assurance on the council's financial forecast and savings delivery capability.
findings.figures: 4 audits deferred; these areas were identified for prioritisation through the 2026/27 Internal Audit Plan
findings.quote: Four audits originally included in the 2025/26 plan were deferred to 2026/27: Financial Sustainability, Budget Management, Savings Assumptions and Plans, and Performance Management. These areas remain significant to the Council's overall risk profile.

findings.paper_title: Updated Head of Internal Audit Opinion
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.thurrock.gov.uk/documents/b21814/Updated Head of Internal Audit Opinion 30th-Jun-2026 19.00 Audit Committee.pdf?T=9
findings.headline: Overall opinion is LIMITED ASSURANCE, indicating material control risks
findings.detail: The Chief Audit Executive issued LIMITED ASSURANCE on the Council's framework of governance, risk management and internal control. The opinion reflects historic control weaknesses and findings from 2025/26 showing a significant number of instances where established controls were not consistently applied in practice.
findings.matters: Limited assurance signals that identified issues, if not addressed, significantly increase the likelihood of risks materialising and objectives not being met. This is a critical governance assessment for credit risk.
findings.figures: 1 audit received No Assurance, 11 received Limited Assurance, 8 received Reasonable Assurance out of 20 completed audits
findings.quote: This reflects the continued impact of historic control and governance weaknesses, together with findings from Internal Audit work in 2025/26 which identified a significant number of instances where established controls were not consistently applied in practice.

findings.headline: All new borrowing requires Commissioner approval, indicating ongoing external financial supervision
findings.detail: The council explicitly requires Commissioner approval for any new borrowing, with the capital refresh mentioning that 'any new borrowing requiring Commissioner approval'. The involvement of Commissioners as approvers of financial decisions indicates the council is under formal intervention or enhanced supervision.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council has autonomous decision-making authority. Commissioner oversight signals that the council is subject to external constraint and that decisions may be reversible or subject to external direction.
findings.figures: Commissioner approval required for new borrowing
findings.quote: reduced reliance on borrowing for the General Fund and for the HRA with any new borrowing requiring Commissioner approval

findings.headline: New governance controls and 'robust business case' requirement introduced for capital projects
findings.detail: The council is implementing new requirements for all capital projects, including mandatory Treasury Management compliance and robust business cases before funding is released. The Commissioner's comments note this is 'the first stage' of a governance framework that 'will need to evolve over time', indicating these are new controls in response to identified weaknesses.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess management quality and internal controls. New governance requirements, especially when introduced retroactively, typically indicate previous failures in project selection or financial management that could apply to any credit facility.
findings.figures: New governance requirements effective 2026/27
findings.quote: A robust business case is needed for all new capital projects. Release of funding and approval is contingent on the receipt of a robust business case, which is TM Treasury compliant

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account is moving to significant new borrowing (£5.563m in 2028/29) while drawing down £51m of reserves
findings.detail: HRA is planned to take external borrowing of £0.910m in 2027/28 rising to £5.563m in 2028/29. Over the same three years, HRA reserves are forecast to decline from £18.689m to £14.191m (total drawdown of £51.149m), while also using £21.068m from capital receipts. This combination suggests HRA is becoming cash-constrained.
findings.matters: A lender assessing council sustainability needs to understand HRA financial health. Rapid reserve depletion combined with rising borrowing suggests rents or external funding are insufficient to cover capital maintenance and debt service, which would eventually flow through to the general fund.
findings.figures: HRA External Borrowing 2028/29: £5.563m; HRA Reserves declining from £18.689m to £14.191m; Reserves drawdown total £51.149m over three years
findings.quote: Financing - Housing Revenue Account... External Borrowing... 0.000 0.910 5.563... Reserves 18.689 18.269 14.191

findings.headline: Capital receipts from asset sales are being diverted to debt repayment, not capital funding
findings.detail: The council had assumed capital receipts of £8.293m would fund capital projects, but has determined that all capital receipts from divestments and asset disposals must instead be applied to debt reduction. Switching any funding source to borrowing requires Commissioner approval, which constrains the council's financial flexibility.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand debt trajectory. When a council prioritizes debt repayment over capital investment, it signals either debt stress or external pressure to deleverage. The requirement for Commissioner approval indicates the council is under external financial supervision.
findings.figures: £8.293m capital receipts (reduced to £7.844m after adjustments) redirected to debt reduction
findings.quote: all capital receipts received through divestments and asset disposals are to be applied to debt reduction. To switch the funding source from capital receipt to prudential borrowing requires Commissioner approval

findings.headline: £3 million borrowing requirement identified but approval deferred due to slippage concerns
findings.detail: The capital refresh identified a residual £3.003m of additional borrowing required for years 2027/28 and 2028/29. However, the council has explicitly declined to recommend approval of this borrowing because of the high slippage reported at Q3. This creates an unresolved funding gap that will need to be revisited.
findings.matters: A lender needs clarity on future funding needs. A deferred-but-not-eliminated borrowing requirement signals unresolved financial pressure and suggests additional borrowing will eventually be required, but on uncertain timescales.
findings.figures: £3.003m additional borrowing required 2027/28-2028/29
findings.quote: At this stage the Council is not recommending that £3.003m of additional borrowing be agreed because of the high degree of slippage reported at quarter 3.

findings.headline: General Fund capital programme has delivered only 48% of planned expenditure (52% underspend at Q3)
findings.detail: A significant underspend (£61.780m / 52%) was forecast against the Council's General Fund Capital Programme at quarter 3. The council has introduced a Capital Overview Board and new governance requirements specifically to address this slippage problem, indicating it is a longstanding delivery issue rather than a one-off.
findings.matters: A lender assessing whether the council can execute a capital investment plan needs to understand whether it can actually deliver. A 52% execution rate suggests either unrealistic planning, poor project management, or capability constraints that would apply to any new borrowing.
findings.figures: £61.780m / 52% underspend forecast at Q3 2025/26
findings.quote: At Quarter 3, a significant underspend (£61.780m / 52%) is forecast against the Council's General Fund Capital Programme.

findings.headline: Debt relief from MHCLG/HM Treasury ahead of Local Government Reorganisation is mentioned but not secured
findings.detail: The strategy references 'an element of debt relief to Thurrock ahead of local government reorganisation (LGR)' and relies on it to make the long-term position affordable. However, the amount, timing, and conditions are not stated—only that MHCLG/HM Treasury 'have committed'. This is a political decision, not a contractual obligation.
findings.matters: The entire 2027/29 forecast assumes debt relief that is not yet quantified or secured. If negotiations fail, or if LGR is delayed or cancelled, the council's path becomes unaffordable. This introduces significant political and timing risk.
findings.figures: MHCLG/HM Treasury committed to provide 'an element of debt relief' before LGR, but no figures or timeline stated
findings.quote: MHCLG /HM Treasury have committed to provide an element of debt relief to Thurrock ahead of local government reorganisation (LGR).

findings.headline: Divestment of £0.9bn failed commercial portfolio is critical to plan; execution risk marked AMBER
findings.detail: The entire recovery strategy depends on selling the council's commercial property portfolio (bought under failed investment initiative) to generate capital receipts that reduce debt. The strategy explicitly names this as an AMBER risk: 'may be lower or unpredictable in timings leading to higher costs'. Market conditions, buyer appetite, or valuations could deteriorate.
findings.matters: If divestment proceeds fall short or delay, the council cannot hit its CFR reduction targets and will need further government support or more rapid service cuts. The plan is built on an assumption about asset sales that the council itself judges as uncertain.
findings.figures: £0.9bn commercial investment portfolio; capital receipts forecast 2026/27 £7.8m, 2027/28 £10.7m, 2028/29 £4.1m
findings.quote: Divestment income flows – The Council's treasury management plans are impacted by the expected divestment programme to provide a borrowing need and budgetary costs – These flows may be lower or unpredictable in timings leading to higher costs.

findings.headline: Internal borrowing of £232m is temporary and unsustainable; council using reserves as emergency liquidity
findings.detail: The council is funding £232m of its borrowing need using cash from reserves and working capital rather than external loans. This is explicitly stated as a short-term measure that 'is not expected that this cash position can be sustained into the future'. The council is drawing down reserves to paper over the structural deficit.
findings.matters: Reserves are finite. Once depleted, the council will have no buffer and will be forced to cut services or increase external borrowing immediately. This means the 2028/29 position is more fragile than the CFR figures suggest.
findings.figures: Internal borrowing 2025/26 £232m, forecast to reduce to £102m by 2028/29; CFR exceeds external debt by £232m in 2026/27
findings.quote: At the Council it is not expected that this cash position can be sustained into the future and as a prudent measure the internal borrowing difference between the Council's overall borrowing need, the CFR, and its actual external debt has been reduced by assuming a higher level of external borrowing.

findings.headline: High refinancing risk: majority of £939m debt is short-dated and exposed to rate rises
findings.detail: The council holds £939m external debt forecast for 31/3/27, with a 'relatively short dated' maturity profile. The strategy explicitly notes this 'exhibits risk of an adverse increase in interest rates' and acknowledges that most of the current portfolio will face refinancing at uncertain rates. The council is deliberately maintaining short-term debt pending government debt relief, but this creates exposure if rates remain high.
findings.matters: If interest rates do not fall as forecast, Thurrock faces a cliff: short-term debt matures and must be refinanced at potentially higher rates, escalating annual debt service costs beyond the MTFP. The council has no capacity to absorb this shock.
findings.figures: Actual gross debt on 31/3/26 £846m, forecast 31/3/27 £939m, 31/3/29 £1,037m; debt interest 2026/27 £39.6m
findings.quote: The current debt portfolio structure is relatively short-dated, and exhibits risk of an adverse increase in interest rates which will expose the majority of the current portfolio to higher interest rates and debt management costs.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement rising to £1.139bn by 2028/29 despite recovery plan
findings.detail: The council's total indebtedness (CFR) is forecast to increase from £1.092bn (2025/26) to £1.139bn (2028/29), a rise of £47m. This happens because the annual capitalisation direction (£69-57m) accumulates faster than debt repayment (MRP and capital receipts). The accumulated CD balance is expected to reach £437m by 2028/29, locked into long-term cost.
findings.matters: The council is not deleveraging; it is accumulating more debt from the government's exceptional support mechanism. Each year of deficit spending creates another layer of permanent cost that must be serviced.
findings.quote: the amount of the annual CD is added to the Council's indebtedness (Capital Financing Requirement, CFR). This subsequently attracts further debt interest costs and MRP to the ongoing budget requirement creating further budgetary pressure. The current trajectory of this accumulating process is unaffordable in the future

findings.headline: Council balances budget only through £68.9m government capitalisation direction support
findings.detail: Thurrock cannot balance its operational budget without exceptional financial support from MHCLG/HM Treasury. The net operational deficit is £5.8m, covered entirely by government borrowing permission (capitalisation direction). This means the council is dependent on political agreement year-on-year to remain solvent.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council's revenue position is structurally broken, not cyclically pressured. This is not a temporary tightness; it is a permanent dependency on government forbearance.
findings.figures: £5.8m net deficit between operational budget and core funding in 2026/27; £68.9m capitalisation direction support; £63.1m non-HRA treasury costs
findings.quote: The Council's predicament means the budget can only be balanced by Government EFS through the mechanism of the CD. This means the Council can borrow capital monies to balance the revenue budgetary deficit.

findings.paper_title: Final Revenue Budget 2026/27 and Medium Term Financial Strategy 26/27-28/29
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.thurrock.gov.uk/documents/s51766/Full Council - Revenue Budget 202627 and Final MTFS 202627 to 202829 FINAL.pdf
findings.headline: Demand-led pressures in social care and temporary accommodation continue to overspend despite savings efforts
findings.detail: The paper notes that pressures remain in 'demand-led placement costs in Adult Social Care and Children's Services, and in temporary accommodation services' and that 'Pressures experienced in year influence the setting of future year budgets.' The 2025/26 budget forecast shows significant treasury underspends but ongoing service pressures. The council continues to see growth allocations for temporary accommodation (originally reduced by £1.614m from draft but still present in final budget), indicating unresolved demand management.
findings.matters: Persistent demand-led pressures in social care and temporary accommodation indicate the council is facing structural cost increases it cannot control through efficiency savings. These are typically growing service areas nationally, and failure to manage them creates recurring budget gaps.
findings.figures: Temporary accommodation growth revision of -£1.614m from draft (partial mitigation, not full solution); demand-led placements cited as continuing pressure
findings.quote: Pressures remain in demand-led placement costs in Adult Social Care and Children's Services, and in temporary accommodation services. Pressures experienced in year influence the setting of future year budgets.

findings.paper_title: Final Revenue Budget 2026/27 and Medium Term Financial Strategy 26/27-28/29
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.thurrock.gov.uk/documents/s51766/Full Council - Revenue Budget 202627 and Final MTFS 202627 to 202829 FINAL.pdf
findings.headline: Fair Funding 2.0 creates £0.680m funding loss in 2027/28 with no mitigation plan
findings.detail: Changes announced in the Final Local Government Finance Settlement on 9 February 2026 regarding business rates pooling will result in a loss of £1.345m in Revenue Support Grant for 2026/27 (offset by a one-year Adjustment Support Grant of £1.345m), but the loss of £0.680m in 2027/28 is not mitigated. The government has not yet announced mitigation for 2028/29. This creates an identified funding gap in the medium term that the council will need to address, either through further savings or drawdown of reserves.
findings.matters: An unmitigated funding loss of £0.680m in 2027/28 represents a known future budget pressure. Combined with the other pressures in the MTFS, this reduces the council's financial flexibility and increases the likelihood of further exceptional support requests.
findings.figures: RSG loss 2026/27 £1.345m (mitigated); RSG loss 2027/28 £0.680m (unmitigated); no mitigation for 2028/29
findings.quote: This alters authorities 2025/26 starting baselines, affecting transitional protections and hence the Fair Funding Assessment (FFA) for 2026/27 and 2027/28. This change to the transitional arrangements is made through the Revenue Support Grant (RSG). This results in a loss of RSG for Thurrock Council of £1.345m in 2026/27 and £0.680m in 2027/28. There is no change to the 2028/29 indicative allocation... There is no mitigation yet for 2027/28

findings.paper_title: Final Revenue Budget 2026/27 and Medium Term Financial Strategy 26/27-28/29
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.thurrock.gov.uk/documents/s51766/Full Council - Revenue Budget 202627 and Final MTFS 202627 to 202829 FINAL.pdf
findings.headline: 6% of 2025/26 savings (£1.173m) have been rated unachievable in year, raising questions about delivery of £13.9m 2026/27 savings target
findings.detail: Of the £18.966m savings planned for 2025/26, only 84% are on track to be delivered. At Quarter 3 (end December 2025), £1.173m (6%) have been rated as unachievable in year. While the council is tracking savings delivery and proactively developing mitigation plans, the fact that savings are slipping even as the year progresses indicates implementation risk. The council has set a £13.938m savings target for 2026/27 but has not yet demonstrated it can consistently deliver planned savings.
findings.matters: Savings failures indicate either over-optimistic planning or weak implementation capability. If the council cannot deliver projected savings, it will face further budget gaps and increased reliance on reserves or further EFS. This pattern weakens confidence in the financial projections.
findings.figures: 2025/26 savings target £18.966m; at Q3, £1.173m (6%) unachievable; 2026/27 savings target £13.938m
findings.quote: At Quarter 3 no schemes are deemed to be 'at risk' and only 6% of the savings (£1.173m) have been rated as unachievable, which are addressed in the 2026/27 budget.

findings.paper_title: Final Revenue Budget 2026/27 and Medium Term Financial Strategy 26/27-28/29
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.thurrock.gov.uk/documents/s51766/Full Council - Revenue Budget 202627 and Final MTFS 202627 to 202829 FINAL.pdf
findings.headline: Operating deficit of £5.8m in 2026/27 is only offset through Capitalisation Direction
findings.detail: Once treasury costs are excluded, the council's operating budget shows a shortfall of £5.828m in 2026/27. This is the gap between core funding (£198.383m) and operating expenditure (£204.210m after £13.938m savings). Rather than being resolved through further service reductions, this gap is being funded through the Capitalisation Direction. This indicates the council is at the limits of what savings it can deliver operationally.
findings.matters: An operational deficit that cannot be closed through savings or service reductions suggests the council's service base is unsustainable at current funding levels. It indicates the council is dependent on government bailout not just for legacy debt, but for current operations.
findings.figures: Operating budget shortfall (Shortfall/Surplus to CD) in 2026/27 is £5.828m; core funding £198.383m vs operating budget £204.210m
findings.quote: Shortfall/(Surplus) to CD... 2026/27: 5.828m

findings.paper_title: Final Revenue Budget 2026/27 and Medium Term Financial Strategy 26/27-28/29
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.thurrock.gov.uk/documents/s51766/Full Council - Revenue Budget 202627 and Final MTFS 202627 to 202829 FINAL.pdf
findings.headline: External debt of £846m with Capital Financing Requirement rising to £1.139bn by 2028/29
findings.detail: As of 31 March 2026, estimated external debt is £846m. The Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) is estimated at £1.092bn for 31/03/26, rising to £1.139bn by 31 March 2029. The council is using internal borrowing (cash reserves) of £0.232m at 31 March 2026 to offset some external borrowing need, but this provides limited headroom. The debt servicing costs (treasury costs) are forecast at £63.080m for 2026/27 and rising to £68.747m by 2028/29.
findings.matters: The absolute debt levels are high and rising. The council's debt servicing costs consume significant portions of its budget and are forecast to increase. Rising CFR indicates ongoing structural deficits being financed through borrowing rather than resolved through operational improvements.
findings.figures: External debt £846m (31/03/26), CFR £1.092bn (31/03/26) rising to £1.139bn (31/03/29); internal borrowing £0.232m; treasury costs 2026/27 £63.080m, 2028/29 £68.747m
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2026, the council's estimated level of external debt is £846m. The Council's debt requirement (capital financing requirement) is estimated to be £1.092bn by the 31/03/26 increasing to £1.139m by the end of 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Final Revenue Budget 2026/27 and Medium Term Financial Strategy 26/27-28/29
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.thurrock.gov.uk/documents/s51766/Full Council - Revenue Budget 202627 and Final MTFS 202627 to 202829 FINAL.pdf
findings.headline: Business rates baseline reset reduced retained business rates income by £14.4m in a single year
findings.detail: Fair Funding 2.0 has reset the business rates baseline that Thurrock can retain. Retained business rates fell from £60.428m in 2025/26 to £46.012m in 2026/27. This is a one-year cliff-edge decline driven by the removal of a £3.198m collection fund surplus used in 2025/26 plus an increase in the tariff Thurrock pays into the national pool as a result of the reset. Unlike other funding changes, this reduction is not phased over three years, creating a material income shock.
findings.matters: A sudden £14.4m reduction in a major revenue stream signals reduced financial flexibility and increases reliance on other funding sources. It demonstrates the volatility of the council's income base and vulnerability to policy changes beyond its control.
findings.figures: Business rates retention fell from £60.428m (2025/26) to £46.012m (2026/27); collection fund surplus removal £3.198m; change occurring in one year, not phased
findings.quote: The removal of the collection fund surplus of £3.198m that supported the 2025/26 budget, and the impact of the national business rates reset leading to an increase in the tariff that Thurrock Council pays into the national pool. This reduction occurs I one year and is not phased over three years.

findings.paper_title: Final Revenue Budget 2026/27 and Medium Term Financial Strategy 26/27-28/29
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.thurrock.gov.uk/documents/s51766/Full Council - Revenue Budget 202627 and Final MTFS 202627 to 202829 FINAL.pdf
findings.headline: Accumulated DSG deficit forecast to reach £46.1m by 2028/29, with the council ultimately responsible for 10% after statutory override ends
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) accumulated deficit is currently £6.459m and is forecast to grow to £46.091m by the end of 2028/29. The statutory override protecting councils from recording this as a real budget shortfall ends in March 2028. The government has announced it will cover up to 90% of the historic DSG deficit accumulated by 2026/27 through a High Needs Stability Grant, but the council will be responsible for the remaining 10% plus any deficits accrued in 2026/27 and 2027/28.
findings.matters: The DSG deficit represents a substantial future liability that could impact the council's financial sustainability. While the override provides temporary protection, the council may face a significant balance sheet hit in 2028 and responsibility for ongoing deficits in SEND spending that it cannot control.
findings.figures: 2025/26 accumulated deficit £6.459m, forecast 2028/29 deficit £46.091m; High Needs Block budget required £54.305m against allocation of £44.035m (£10.270m shortfall in 2026/27)
findings.quote: The accumulated deficit is forecast to grow by 2028/29 to an estimated at £46.091m. Whilst the statutory override remains in place, the deficit is held against the Council's reserves... the 10% remaining deficit will fall to local authorities to cover

findings.paper_title: Final Revenue Budget 2026/27 and Medium Term Financial Strategy 26/27-28/29
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.thurrock.gov.uk/documents/s51766/Full Council - Revenue Budget 202627 and Final MTFS 202627 to 202829 FINAL.pdf
findings.headline: Council cannot balance its budget without £68.9m exceptional financial support from central government
findings.detail: Thurrock requires an indicative Capitalisation Direction of £68.908m for 2026/27 to set a legally balanced budget. The council's core funding is £198.383m but its total budget requirement is £267.291m. Without this exceptional support, the council cannot meet its statutory obligation to set a balanced budget. This dependency has persisted for several years and is expected to continue through the medium term.
findings.matters: A council dependent on exceptional financial support to balance its budget presents material credit risk. The lender is effectively funding the gap between the council's revenues and its essential expenditures, with repayment uncertain.
findings.figures: Core funding £198.383m, Budget requirement £267.291m, EFS required £68.908m; total EFS requirement over seven years (2022/23-2028/29) is £637.574m, down from £691.280m forecast in February 2025
findings.quote: The Council's financial position remains exponentially challenging and will be so for several years with the Council requiring exceptional financial support (EFS), from central government, to achieve its legal requirement to set a balanced budget for the forthcoming year.

news_drafts.headline: Remaining divestment and asset disposal resources forecast insufficient to reduce borrowing without additional government support
news_drafts.lead: There is no self-help path to sustainability. The council is entirely dependent on whether government support continues beyond current commitments.

news_drafts.headline: Financing costs consume one-third of non-HRA revenue, leaving minimal capacity for service spending or reserve building
news_drafts.lead: One-third of revenue consumed by debt servicing is a stark indicator of unaffordability. No service improvements or reserves accumulation is possible when legacy debt dominates the budget.

news_drafts.headline: Major asset sales (wind farm disposals c£40m) slipped from 2024/25 to 2026/27, delaying reduction in the borrowing requirement
news_drafts.lead: Disposal slippage directly extends the period of government dependence and increases the risk that conditions for the £200m relief package cannot be met. Further slippage would materially worsen the financial outlook.
